Brightness
BRITE-nes
n. (radiance, effulgence; rendering Hebrew nogahh, zohar, Greek apaugasma, epiphaneia)
Old English beorhtnes, from beorht, shining, clear. In Scripture the word is almost always theological: it names the visible outshining of the glory of God, and in Hebrews it names the Son's relation to the Father.

Biblical Definition

Brightness is the shining-forth of glory, and the New Testament uses it to state one of the most precise Christological claims in Scripture: the Son is “the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person” (Hebrews 1:3). The Greek is apaugasma, the radiance that streams from a light source — not a lamp lit from another lamp, which would be a second and later thing, but the shining that is coeval with and inseparable from the light itself. This is the language the Nicene fathers reached for in light of light, very God of very God, and it is why eternal generation is not a speculation but an exegesis: a light is never without its radiance. In the Old Testament the word attends the appearances of God. Ezekiel, groping for words at the end of his vision, says “so was the appearance of the brightness round about. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD” (Ezekiel 1:28) — and falls on his face. Isaiah makes it eschatological and missionary at once: “the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising” (Isaiah 60:3). And Paul makes it the instrument of judgment: the man of sin is destroyed “with the brightness of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8). The same radiance that draws the nations annihilates the antichrist; brightness saves and brightness kills, depending on what it falls upon.

Webster 1828 Definition

The outshining of glory. Hebrews 1:3 makes it the technical term for the Son's eternal relation to the Father; Ezekiel falls on his face before it; Isaiah says kings will come to it; Paul says it destroys the Wicked one.

expand to see more

BRIGHTNESS, n. [See Bright.] Splendor; luster; glitter; as the brightness of the sun.

2. Acuteness, applied to the faculties; sharpness of wit; as the brightness of a man's parts.

3. In Scripture, the visible effulgence attending the manifested glory of God; as the brightness of his rising. Is. 60.

4. That which shines forth from a luminous body, inseparable from the body itself.

5. Clearness; freedom from obscurity or dimness.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 1:3 — "Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;"

Ezekiel 1:28 — "As the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness round about. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face, and I heard a voice of one that spake."

Isaiah 60:3 — "And the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising."

2 Thessalonians 2:8 — "And then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming:"

Modern Corruption

Hebrews 1:3 is read as a poetic compliment rather than a metaphysical statement, and the eternal generation of the Son that it teaches is treated as optional speculation — leaving the door open to the subordinationism the word was chosen to shut.

expand to see more

The whole force of apaugasma is that radiance is not made, not adopted, and not later. Arius taught that there was when the Son was not; the writer of Hebrews had already answered him by three centuries with a metaphor that cannot be pried apart. You cannot have the glory without the brightness, nor date the brightness after the glory. When modern treatments soften this into imagery about Jesus reflecting God's character, the metaphor is quietly reversed — a reflection is a separate surface receiving borrowed light, which is precisely what apaugasma denies. The dictionary holds the Nicene and confessional position without hedging: the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, of one substance with Him, and Hebrews 1:3 is one of the load-bearing texts.

A second and lesser drift affects Isaiah 60:3 and 2 Thessalonians 2:8, which are frequently split apart as though brightness were a merely comforting category. Scripture will not allow the separation. The nations walk to the brightness and the antichrist is consumed by it in the same divine outshining, exactly as the pillar of fire lit Israel and troubled the Egyptians in one night (Exodus 14:20). The light does not change; the relation to it does. Any account of God's glory that can only warm and never wound has taken half a Bible.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nogahh (shining, radiance) and zohar (brilliance); Greek apaugasma (effulgence streaming from a source) and epiphaneia (appearing, manifestation).

expand to see more

Hebrew nogahh (H5051) — brightness, shining; used of the LORD's theophanic light in 2 Samuel 22:13 and Ezekiel 1:28.

Hebrew zohar (H2096) — brilliance, splendour; used in Daniel 12:3 of the wise shining as the brightness of the firmament.

Greek apaugasma (G541) — effulgence, radiance issuing from a light source; the hapax of Hebrews 1:3.

Greek epiphaneia (G2015) — appearing, manifestation; the word rendered brightness in 2 Thessalonians 2:8 and elsewhere appearing.

Greek charakter (G5481) — the exact impress of a die, the companion term in Hebrews 1:3 rendered express image.

Usage

"“The brightness of his glory” — not a reflection of God but the outshining of God, inseparable from the source."

"“Kings to the brightness of thy rising” — the missionary pull of God's glory shining on His people."

"“Destroy with the brightness of his coming” — the same radiance is the end of the man of sin."
